title: A generic “Preserve Editorial Intent” rule can break the editorial hierarchy — the experiment that proves it
description: Adding a non‑specific editorial‑hierarchy instruction to the Narrative prompt did not preserve the intended company‑first message; instead it systematically reduced Nuëyon’s company identity and audience emphasis, elevated orchestration to the central positioning, and introduced unsupported audience/validation claims — producing a measurable regression and a rollback decision.
audience: Prompt engineers, narrative editors, product communications leads, and anyone who writes or vets editorial system prompts.
rationale: This is the clearest, highest‑value story the source supports: a targeted change to a Narrative user prompt caused predictable, repeatable editorial drift and failed hard editorial gates, so the candidate prompt was rejected. It matters because teams often add generic guardrails hoping to protect intent; this experiment shows that an underspecified, reusable rule can instead change what an agent emphasizes. Gaps/uncertainties: the report does not establish why the generic rule caused the drift (e.g., specific phrasing, model backend behavior, or interaction with the existing Synthesis wording), nor whether a different formulation would succeed. The experiment used three runs per condition without temperature/seed control, so statistical generalization is limited.
evidence:
• Candidate prompt added a section titled “Preserve Editorial Intent from the Synthesis.”
• Narrative mean score fell from 6.00 (baseline) to 4.00 (candidate); Compose mean fell from 5.67 to 3.33.
• All three candidate Narrative and Compose runs failed the Theme Hierarchy gate (C) and the Factual/Editorial Restraint gate (D).
• Candidate outputs made orchestration central and introduced unsupported claims (validation intent, named audience of founders/product leaders).
• Decision: “Do not promote.” Production prompt restored byte‑for‑byte (rollback SHA matches baseline).
